title: Olympics updates: Canada’s through! Plus: Alysa Liu’s swag
content:
Games Briefing 🏅 | This is The Athletic’s daily newsletter for the Milan Cortina Olympics. Sign up here to receive the Games Briefing directly in your inbox.

MILAN — We’re almost there. The men’s hockey gold medal game is less than 48 hours away. Who will play in it? We’re working on that.

We at least know one of the teams: Canada beat Finland in a(nother) wild game just now. The Canadians took their first lead of the semifinal, 3-2, with 35 seconds left to play. They advanced without the help of their captain, Sidney Crosby, who was sidelined with injury.

In a few hours, the Americans are up against Slovakia. Follow our live blog for updates.

Also in today’s edition:

🤘 Alysa Liu’s shine

🇳🇴 Record for Norway

🇮🇹 Italy’s success

To stay on top of everything throughout Italy, 📲 stick with our ongoing live coverage and 📅 customize your schedule by day and by sport, tailored to your time zone.

American figure skater Alysa Liu said she didn’t need a medal to be happy. She was back skating at age 20 after taking time away. Ever since her return, her light-hearted, free-spirited way has radiated off her. But she couldn’t really be this chill about the Olympics, could she?

Turns out, she was. And it worked. Liu delivered a dazzling free skate Thursday night to jump two spots in the standings and return the U.S. to the top of the women’s figure skating Olympic podium for the first time since 2002. She was bursting with joy the whole night.

One of you put it best:

And so much of that joy is about where she’s from, and how the sum of her experiences has molded her into an athlete with enough confidence to reject some of the most classic assumptions about her sport.

However she carries it forward, it’s clear that her victory is already an inspiration for figure skating in the United States.

“There’s gonna be so many little kids showing up for little learn-to-skate programs everywhere in the country because of Alysa,” Liu’s coach Phillip DiGuglielmo said.

🇳🇴 Norway broke its own record for most medals in a single Winter Olympics.

🇮🇹 Italy is having itself quite a good home Olympics. How’d it do it? Money, a “ghost” and a little luck.

🥌 The men’s curling gold medal game will be a heavyweight fight between top-ranked Great Britain and familiar powerhouse Canada. On the women’s side, it’s Sweden versus Switzerland; the U.S. will play Canada for bronze.

🗞️ Fun one here: In the Dolomites, the Olympics get translated into Ladin, the Alps’ oldest language.

🛷 It’s very expensive to send bobsleds around the world. And it’s a particularly large problem for Team USA.

📷 The New York Times has a cool, interactive look at all of Liu’s jumps from the women’s singles figure skating competition.

Reminder: All of The Athletic’s Olympics coverage is free to read in our app.

Some of you have emailed us to ask us a key question: How’s the food, and what are we eating? Our U.S. and U.K. colleagues have been asking us the same, too, and the truth is that the schedule is making it so that we really appreciate the moments we’re not eating in a rush or finding whatever we can after some lengthy events. That’s not a complaint, by any means — we are all massively lucky to get to bring you everything that’s happening here.

And there are definitely times we get to eat some great food, like this ravioli with ossobuco and a little risotto inside:

This was from a joint called Il Piccolo — it translates to “The Little One” in English — and one of the perks of it along with being delicious is that it was near the Milan cauldron.

At night this late into the Games is an amazing time to see the Olympic flame. It’s bustling but not crowded, mostly folks finishing up dinner or their evenings and strolling nearby, wanting to give a look to one of the most enduring symbols of the Olympics. And this cauldron’s setting at the Arco della Pace gives it a feel of integration within the city that is sometimes absent at other Games.
